design_detail: Two between-group experiments in rats, designed as a replication of Alexander et al. (1981), one of the 'Rat Park' studies. In each experiment 10 male and 10 female outbred Wistar rats (Charles River Canada) were raised from weaning (21 days) alone in standard cages and 10 males and 10 females together in an 8.8 m² colony box. From 113 to 142 days of age all rats had 24-h access to tap water and a second fluid in seven 4-day phases: 10% sucrose; 10% sucrose with 0.05 mg/ml quinine sulfate (a bitter-sweet control); morphine hydrochloride at 1.0, 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125 mg/ml in 10% sucrose; 10% sucrose again. Experiment 1 recorded each colony rat's drinking with a computer-controlled, video-identified dispenser reached by climbing a pole; Experiment 2 removed the pole and the automated system and weighed communal reservoirs, so colony intake was known only as a group total. Isolated rats drank from weighed bottles in both experiments. Every finding is in rats.
can_establish: That in these two cohorts of Wistar rats from a later breeding stock, colony housing did not lower intake of sweetened morphine solution compared with isolation: in Experiment 1 colony rats drank slightly more at 1.0 mg/ml and no differently at the lower concentrations.
cannot_establish: Why the earlier result was not reproduced (the strain-change explanation was not tested: no rats from the earlier stock were run), the title's claim that environment matters less than other variables (genes were not manipulated), anything about individual colony rats in Experiment 2 (only reservoir totals), or anything about addiction in people.

sample.recruitment: Laboratory animals: outbred Wistar rats of Charles River Canada origin, raised from weaning (21 days) in their housing condition, tested from 113 to 142 days of age and killed at 143 days (p. 392, Experiment 1 › Method › Subjects; p. 393, Procedure; p. 396, Experiment 2 › Method › Subjects). Experiment 2 used a new set of rats (the first set was killed at the end of Experiment 1).
sample.demographics: Equal numbers of males and females in every condition; body weights taken at 114 and 142 days but not reported.
sample.attrition: Not reported. The degrees of freedom of the Experiment 1 analyses fit 38 and then 37 rats rather than 40 (see reporting issues).
sample.selection_effects: One supplier and stock; how rats were allocated to housing is not described; colony rats of both sexes lived together from weaning for about four months, and pregnancies or litters are not mentioned. The paper gives no dates for its experiments; the personal communications it cites are dated May 1985 (pp. 398–399) and it was accepted in January 1996 (p. 400).

exposure.measurement: Fluid weights. Isolated rats: two bottles fastened outside each cage, weighed, with bottles on two empty cages to correct for spillage and evaporation (p. 392). Colony, Experiment 1: a computer-controlled system weighed each of two fluids drunk at every visit (0.1 g resolution), identified the rat from a video of its hair-dye mark, and could be reached only by climbing a 41-cm pole (pp. 392–393). Colony, Experiment 2: two communal reservoirs weighed daily, with untouched control reservoirs for evaporation; individual intake unknown (p. 396).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions in rats: oral, voluntary, 24-h choice beside tap water, 4 days per phase, bottle sides swapped every 2 days; morphine hydrochloride at 1.0, 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125 mg/ml in 10% sucrose (16 days in all, in descending order), after a 10% sucrose phase and a quinine–sucrose phase and before a final sucrose phase (Table 1, p. 394; Procedure, p. 393). The quinine–sucrose solution was chosen because it tasted, to people, like the 0.25 mg/ml morphine solution (p. 393).
exposure.polysubstance: None: one drug, and the rats had no previous morphine exposure (p. 392).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: morphine-naive at the start; no withdrawal or abstinence tests.

comparison.controls: Isolated rats in standard 18 × 25 × 18 cm cages with sheet-metal walls preventing visual contact, against colony rats in an open-topped wooden box (8.8 m²) with cedar shavings and two open metal cages holding the feeders, in each experiment; sucrose-only phases (1 and 7) and the quinine phase (2) as taste controls (pp. 392–393).
comparison.matching: Same supplier, strain and age; equal sex numbers; shared lighting on one timer (p. 393).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measure before housing began; allocation method not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Experiment 1: per phase, the proportion of experimental fluid to total fluid, mg of experimental substance per kg body weight, grams of experimental fluid, and total fluid in grams (p. 393, Results, 1st paragraph); means in Table 2 (p. 395). Experiment 2: group average daily grams of each fluid (Table 3, p. 397).
outcomes.validity_norms: The automated system was introduced because the older Rat Park apparatus was unreliable (eight days of data lost in Alexander et al. 1981, p. 392); its accuracy against weighed bottles is not reported here (it is said to be described in Petrie et al. 1985).
outcomes.operationalization: Morphine consumption = intake of sweetened morphine solution beside water; no measure of dependence, withdrawal or motivation.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Stated as two-way repeated-measures ANOVAs corrected for multiple comparisons, without naming the method, run separately for each of 7 phases and 4 measures (28 analyses, each testing housing, sex and their interaction), followed by Newman–Keuls comparisons; only p<.05 is reported (pp. 393–394). The count of 28 is the editors'. Experiment 2: no inferential test.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; housing cannot be hidden from staff who weighed bottles and reservoirs.

analysis.effect_sizes: Average daily grams without SDs. Experiment 1 (Table 2, p. 395), experimental fluid, isolated vs colony: sucrose pretest 103.2 vs 108.3; quinine 33.4 vs 75.0; morphine 1.0 mg/ml 0.0 vs 3.6; 0.5 mg/ml 0.5 vs 1.3; 0.25 mg/ml 15.7 vs 18.3; 0.125 mg/ml 30.2 vs 42.8; sucrose posttest 81.4 vs 79.6. Colony more than isolated in the 1.0 mg/ml phase on all four measures (proportion F(1, 34)=55.2; grams F(1, 34)=80.98; total fluid F(1, 34)=11.4; mg/kg significant, statistic not printed); no housing difference at 0.5, 0.25 or 0.125 mg/ml (pp. 394–395). Females more than males in mg/kg in all four morphine phases (F 6.1, 12.1, 4.7 and 5.7, p<.05; p. 394). Experiment 2 (Table 3, p. 397), isolated vs colony: 1.0 mg/ml 0.3 vs 4.3; 0.5 mg/ml 9.4 vs 3.0; 0.25 mg/ml 17.4 vs 10.9; 0.125 mg/ml 44.4 vs 33.1; quinine 26.3 vs 10.4; no test. Editors' calculation (treating 1 g of solution as about 1 ml): mean daily morphine hydrochloride intake was 0 and 0.3 mg in isolated rats and 3.6 and 4.3 mg in colony rats at 1.0 mg/ml, between 0.25 and 4.7 mg across groups at 0.5 mg/ml, and between 2.7 and 5.6 mg in every group at 0.25 and 0.125 mg/ml.
analysis.covariates: None; sex entered as a factor.
analysis.selective_reporting: mg/kg values and body weights are never shown, although mg/kg carries the sex differences and the Phase 3 housing difference; no SDs or individual data; non-significant effects are not reported with statistics.
analysis.power: Not reported; 10 rats per sex per housing condition in each experiment.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In two cohorts measured with different colony methods, colony housing did not reduce intake of sweetened morphine solution. Experiment 1 found colony rats drinking slightly more at 1.0 mg/ml (3.6 vs 0.0 g a day) and no difference at lower concentrations. Experiment 2, without a test, showed colony rats drinking more at 1.0 mg/ml and less at 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125 mg/ml, by margins smaller than the up-to-sevenfold differences the author cites for Alexander et al. (1981). Both groups drank far less of every morphine solution than of plain sucrose.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title says environment is not the most important variable in oral morphine consumption, and the summary attributes the non-replication to strain differences introduced when the supplier changed its breeding colony (p. 391); the conclusion calls the confounding factors most likely genetic (p. 399). Neither genes nor stock were tested: the evidence is a date (the 1981 study ran April–July 1979; the stock changed in November 1979), personal communications, and one study of amphetamine-induced activity in the two stocks (pp. 398–399). Experiment 2 is called consistent with Experiment 1 (p. 397), though in three of four morphine phases its isolated rats drank more, the direction of the original finding, and its quinine phase reversed Experiment 1's. The argument that rats drank for the sucrose rather than the morphine (p. 399) is not tested against the quinine control, which was meant for this: in Experiment 1 both groups drank less of the 0.25 mg/ml morphine solution than of the quinine solution said to taste the same (15.7 vs 33.4 g isolated; 18.3 vs 75.0 g colony), though the two phases differ in order.

timeline.event: Alexander, Coambs & Hadaway: isolated rats pretreated with unsweetened morphine drank more morphine solution than colony rats (as described, pp. 391–392).
Hadaway et al.: the same in morphine-naive rats offered progressively more palatable sucrose-morphine solutions (as described, p. 392).

Alexander et al. (published 1981) run April–July 1979 with the supplier's earlier Wistar stock; eight days of data lost to an apparatus fault; in November 1979 the supplier changed its breeding colonies (pp. 392, 398).
This study: two experiments with later-stock Wistar rats do not reproduce lower intake in colony rats.
Gage & Sumnall's critical history of Rat Park summarizes this study as a replication of the 1979 study, although it states it replicated the 1981 study.

replication.where_it_stands: The housing effect on oral morphine intake rests on three small studies from one laboratory and is contradicted by this non-replication; the other housing studies summarized by Gage & Sumnall (2019) point both ways. The strain explanation offered here has not been tested in any study read for this round.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the article.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Single author, Department of Psychology, New Mexico Tech (p. 391). The author is a co-author, with Alexander and Beyerstein of the Rat Park group, of the 1985 chapter that describes the computer-controlled drinking system used in Experiment 1 (reference list, p. 400). Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered replication run in parallel with rats from more than one stock or supplier, randomized to housing, with the same individual automated intake measurement in both housing conditions, sexes housed so that litters cannot confound intake, and prespecified analyses; that would test the housing effect and the strain explanation at once.

domains.note: How weanlings were assigned to isolation or the colony is not described.

Same supplier, stock, age and sex numbers; weights at 114 days were taken but not reported. Plain-sucrose intake in the pretest was similar (103.2 vs 108.3 g in Experiment 1; 116.2 vs 104.5 g in Experiment 2), but housing had already lasted three months.
Housing is the intervention itself; the placement of cages and colony box in the room is not reported, though both shared one lighting timer.

domains.domain: 5. Blinding of caregivers and investigators (performance bias)
domains.note: Housing cannot be hidden from staff, who weighed the isolated rats' bottles and, in Experiment 2, the colony reservoirs; nothing is said about limiting handling differences.
Every rat (or, in Experiment 2, the whole colony) was measured daily throughout.

Unblinded weighing, and in both experiments intake was measured by different methods in the two housing conditions (bottles against an automated dispenser or communal reservoirs), so measurement differences are built into the comparison.
The degrees of freedom imply that two and then three of 40 rats were missing from the Experiment 1 analyses; no reason or group is given.
No protocol (none would be expected at the time); significant effects only are reported with statistics, and mg/kg values, SDs and weights are not shown.

In Experiment 1 colony rats had to climb a 41-cm pole to drink, a cost isolated rats did not face; males and females shared the colony from weaning, with pregnancies not mentioned; Experiment 2 yields only colony totals, so no test was possible.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: SYRCLE defines no overall judgment; this is the editors' summary, set to the most severe judgment among the items that bear on the housing comparison. Allocation is undescribed, weighing was unblinded and done by different methods in the two housing conditions in both experiments (the same weakness the original Rat Park studies are criticized for), colony rats faced an extra effort to drink in Experiment 1, two or three rats are missing from the analyses without explanation, and Experiment 2 could not be tested. Cite the paper for what it found in these two cohorts (no lower intake of sweetened morphine solution in colony-housed rats) and as the published non-replication of Alexander et al. (1981), labelled as a rat finding; do not cite it for the genetic explanation, for the title's claim about environment, or for anything about people.

preclinical.species_strain_sex: Rat; outbred Wistar from Charles River Canada (the supplier's later breeding stock, according to the author); 10 males and 10 females per housing condition in each of two experiments (80 rats); raised from weaning at 21 days; tested at 113–142 days of age.
preclinical.dose_route_schedule: Oral and voluntary: 24-h two-bottle choice between tap water and morphine hydrochloride in 10% sucrose at 1.0, 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125 mg/ml, 4 days each in descending order (16 days of morphine availability), after sucrose and quinine–sucrose phases.
preclinical.human_equivalent_dose_basis: None given by the paper and none calculated here; intake was reported as grams of solution (mg/kg values not shown).
preclinical.resembles_human_use: No. Rats drank a sweetened oral solution with water always available, for 16 days in a fixed descending sequence; no escalation, dependence or withdrawal was measured; cage versus colony is a narrow stand-in for a human social environment.

key_findings.finding: Each experiment used 10 male and 10 female outbred Wistar rats in each housing condition, raised from weaning at 21 days either alone in 18 × 25 × 18 cm cages or together in an 8.8 m² box; from 113 to 142 days of age they chose for 24 h a day between tap water and, in seven 4-day phases, 10% sucrose, 10% sucrose with 0.05 mg/ml quinine sulfate, morphine hydrochloride at 1.0, 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125 mg/ml in 10% sucrose, and 10% sucrose again.
key_findings.locator: Experiment 1 › Method › Subjects and Apparatus (p. 392); Procedure, 1st–5th paragraphs (p. 393); Table 1 (p. 394); Experiment 2 › Method › Subjects (p. 396)

key_findings.finding: Intake was measured differently in the two housing conditions in both experiments: isolated rats drank from bottles weighed against bottles on two empty cages; in Experiment 1 colony rats climbed a 41-cm pole to a computer-controlled dispenser that weighed each visit's intake (0.1 g resolution) and identified the rat by video; in Experiment 2 the pole and the automated system were removed and two communal reservoirs were weighed daily against untouched control reservoirs, so individual colony intake was unknown.
key_findings.locator: Experiment 1 › Method › Apparatus (pp. 392–393); Experiment 2 › Method › Apparatus (p. 396)

key_findings.finding: Experiment 1: colony rats drank more of the experimental fluid relative to water than isolated rats in Phase 2 (quinine; F(1, 34)=32.6), Phase 3 (1.0 mg/ml morphine; F(1, 34)=55.2) and Phase 7 (sucrose; F(1, 33)=11.7); more grams in Phases 2 and 3 (F(1, 34)=18.8 and 80.98); more mg/kg in Phase 3 (statistic not printed); and more total fluid in Phases 2, 3 and 4 (F(1, 34)=6.3 and 11.4; F(1, 33)=17.5); all p<.05. There were no housing differences in morphine consumption in the 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125 mg/ml phases.
key_findings.locator: Experiment 1 › Results, 2nd, 4th and 5th paragraphs (p. 394); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 395)
key_findings.note: Subscripts and some F values are garbled in the PDF's text layer; read on the rendered page at 300 dpi.

key_findings.finding: Experiment 1, average daily grams of experimental fluid, isolated vs colony: sucrose pretest 103.2 vs 108.3; quinine 33.4 vs 75.0; morphine 1.0 mg/ml 0.0 vs 3.6; 0.5 mg/ml 0.5 vs 1.3; 0.25 mg/ml 15.7 vs 18.3; 0.125 mg/ml 30.2 vs 42.8; sucrose posttest 81.4 vs 79.6. Water in the same phases: 2.5 vs 1.3, 26.3 vs 5.5, 39.5 vs 58.8, 44.5 vs 74.6, 33.9 vs 49.5, 23.2 vs 19.6, 8.8 vs 0.7.
key_findings.note: Means only, without SDs or n; checked at 300 dpi.

key_findings.finding: Experiment 1: females drank more mg/kg of experimental fluid than males in Phases 1, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 (F(1, 34)=15.8 and 6.1; F(1, 33)=12.1, 4.7, 5.7 and 14.5; p<.05), that is in all four morphine phases; in Phase 3 colony females drank more mg/kg than each other group, and colony males more than isolated males and females.
key_findings.note: Subscripts are garbled in the PDF's text layer; read on the rendered page at 300 dpi.

key_findings.finding: Experiment 2 (colony intake from communal reservoirs; no inferential test possible): average daily grams of morphine solution, colony vs isolated, 4.3 vs 0.3 at 1.0 mg/ml; isolated vs colony 9.4 vs 3.0 at 0.5 mg/ml, 17.4 vs 10.9 at 0.25 mg/ml and 44.4 vs 33.1 at 0.125 mg/ml. Quinine phase: isolated 26.3, colony 10.4; sucrose pretest 116.2 vs 104.5 and posttest 104.2 vs 94.9.
key_findings.note: The paper does not say how the colony's per-animal averages were derived from the reservoir totals.

key_findings.finding: The author states that the differences in Experiment 2 were never as large as in the rats kept in their original housing in Alexander et al. (1981), where continuously isolated rats drank up to seven times as much sucrose-morphine as continuously colony-housed rats; he concludes that neither experiment replicated the earlier housing research and that the second shows the non-replication was not due to the automated equipment.
key_findings.locator: Experiment 2 › Results, 2nd paragraph (pp. 396–397); Discussion (p. 397); General Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 397)

key_findings.finding: The author locates the difference in the isolated rats: they drank much less sucrose-morphine than the isolated rats of Alexander et al. (1981), whereas colony rats drank similar amounts in all three studies, although the 1981 rats drank less plain sucrose (Phases 1 and 7) than the present rats.

Proposed explanation, not tested: the 1981 study was run April–July 1979, and in November 1979 the supplier changed its outbred Wistar breeding colonies, so the earlier rats were Old Colony and the present ones New Colony Wistars. Support offered: the supplier's reasons for the change (personal communication, May 1985), reports of lower voluntary alcohol intake in New Colony Wistars (two personal communications, May 1985), and one study (Ton et al. 1983) in which chronic naltrexone affected amphetamine-induced activity differently in Old and New Colony male rats. No Old Colony rats were tested.

The author argues that, across all three studies, rats did not increase their morphine intake over time but drank more of the solution as its morphine content fell, consuming about the same absolute amount of morphine, and so drank it for the sucrose; he calls the data a strong disconfirmation of the natural-affinity hypothesis (Goldstein 1972, 1976).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Tables 2 and 3 (treating 1 g of solution as about 1 ml): mean daily morphine hydrochloride intake was 0 and 0.3 mg in isolated rats and 3.6 and 4.3 mg in colony rats at 1.0 mg/ml, 0.25 to 4.7 mg across groups at 0.5 mg/ml, and 2.7 to 5.6 mg in every group at 0.25 and 0.125 mg/ml, so it was roughly constant only across the last two morphine phases; mg/kg values are not printed.

key_findings.finding: The drinking apparatus of the earlier studies was unreliable: in Alexander et al. (1981) an electronic fault lost eight days of data, so only three-quarters of the potential data could be analysed; the computer-controlled system was introduced for this reason, and no data were lost to equipment in Experiment 1.

reporting_issues.issue: Experiment 1 had 20 isolated and 20 colony rats, but its ANOVAs report F with 1 and 34 df in Phases 1–3 and 1 and 33 df in Phases 4–7 (post hoc df 34 and 33 likewise); by the editors' calculation, 40 rats in a 2 (housing) × 2 (sex) design give 36 error df, so 38 and then 37 rats were analysed, and no death, loss or exclusion is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Two or three rats were dropped from the analyses for unstated reasons and from unknown groups; with 10 rats per cell this could matter for the sex-by-housing comparisons.

reporting_issues.issue: Experiment 2 is called consistent with Experiment 1, but in three of its four morphine phases its isolated rats drank more morphine solution than its colony rats (9.4 vs 3.0, 17.4 vs 10.9 and 44.4 vs 33.1 g), the direction of the original finding, whereas in Experiment 1 colony rats drank as much or more in every morphine phase; the quinine phase also reversed (colony 75.0 vs isolated 33.4 g in Experiment 1; colony 10.4 vs isolated 26.3 g in Experiment 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: The two experiments agree only in that neither shows a difference as large as the earlier study's; the reversal between colony measurement methods suggests that the method affected the results, which the paper does not discuss.

reporting_issues.issue: No standard deviations, individual data, body weights or mg/kg values are reported; the F statistic for the colony–isolated mg/kg difference in Phase 3 is not printed; and the method of the stated correction for multiple comparisons is not named.
reporting_issues.consequence: Effect sizes cannot be computed, and the claim about constant absolute morphine intake can be checked only roughly from grams of solution.

reporting_issues.issue: The General Discussion says rats kept consuming about the same absolute amount of morphine as the concentration fell, but by the editors' calculation from Tables 2 and 3 daily morphine intake was near zero in isolated rats at 1.0 mg/ml (0 and 0.3 mg) and below 1 mg in both Experiment 1 groups at 0.5 mg/ml, and about 2.7–5.6 mg in all groups only in the last two morphine phases.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sucrose-not-morphine reading rests on a pattern the tables show only at the lowest concentrations; avoidance of the stronger solutions fits the data at least as well.

reporting_issues.issue: The non-replication is attributed to a change of breeding stock in November 1979, but the paper gives no dates for its own experiments; the personal communications it cites are dated May 1985, and it was accepted in January 1996 (date printed at the foot of p. 400, absent from the PDF's text layer).
reporting_issues.consequence: When the experiments were run is unknown; claims should date the failed replication by its publication (1996), not by when the work was done.
